title: The 1961 Experimental Canadian Short Film that Inspired Kubrick's Dr. Strangelove.

commenti.body: George Lucas also quite liked Lipsett. He seems to have become aware of his films - "Very Nice, Very Nice" and "21-87" - after he finished film-school and engaged in some classes in the school's graduate program. Its influence is somewhat apparent in Lucas' THX-1138 (both the student film and the feature film), both of which quote both titles.

For those curious, the *21-87* and *THX-1138* references in *Star Wars* occur during the cell block sequence when Luke says, “Prisoner transfer from cell block 1148,” and when Han says, “Now we just have to find out what cell this princess of yours is in. Here it is. 2187. You go and get her, I'll hold them here.”

In *The Force Awakens*, Finn’s stormtrooper serial number is FN-2187, but I’d imagine this is a callback to the original *Star Wars* rather than to Lipsett’s short film.

THX-1138 - the student film more than the feature film - also takes on something of the style of Lipsett, although its perhaps more indebted to Slavko Vorkapich's *The Life and Death of 9413: a Hollywood Extra*. Vorkapich was a former dean of the faculty Lucas studied in and his works were quite popular in the student body and clearly made an impact on Lucas, probably before he knew of Lipsett's existence.

21-87 does contain a discussion about "a force" but I doubt that much effected Lucas' "Force" in anything but name, if that: these kinds of superpowers were the stuff of pulp sci-fi.

That’s very interesting, Vorkapich’s short has been in watchlist for a few months now — gives me a good reason to watch it sooner rather than later.

But yes, in terms of the frenetic pace of the editing, I definitely agree re: similarities between *THX* and Lipsett. It makes one wonder what sorta films Lucas would’ve made had he not gotten sidetracked becoming one of the most iconic and commercially successful filmmakers of his day.

>It makes one wonder what sorta films Lucas would’ve made had he not gotten sidetracked becoming one of the most iconic and commercially successful filmmakers of his day

I personally don't believe the "Lucas the avant-garde artiste" image that Lucas is clearly interested in projecting. I mean, Coppola was the first to lament the loss that was created by Lucas becoming caught up in Star Wars, but the sorts of films he points out to as the kind of stuff Lucas could have made otherwise, is not THX-1138, its American Graffiti.

Lucas' gigs after film school were mostly in documentary filmmaking, but he also tried to get into features with his stint on the set of McKenna Gold, for example. So his eye was definitely somewhere other than the kind of "tone poems" he prides himself on having made in school.

In fact, if you look at Lucas' shorts, not many of his films fit this "non narrative tone poem" definition. The only ones, in fact, are "Herbie" (which is unsurprising since he made it for a class on film aesthetics) and a short he made on the set of McKenna's gold. Otherwise, his oeuvre is dominated by documentaries and, increasingly, forays into narrative.

Even Lucas' supposed debt to Lipsett and the Canadian avant-garde is smaller than he would like us to think: as I said, its likely Lucas didn't know of Lipsett until after film school, and that his model for his earlier shorts was Vorkapich, instead.

What an interesting coincidence!

I discovered Arthur Lipsett completely at random 2 weeks ago, and wrote about him here https://tilbageidanmark.tumblr.com/post/752212655639494656/ ! I too was very much impressed by his vision and particular way he could juxtapose and edit.

Most of his films are available on YouTube. Worth the dive!

Really great stuff — you’re clearly more informed than I am, so I’ve got little to contribute, nor much to dispute. I’ve only seen *THX* and *Freheit* of Lucas’s short film ouvre.

I guess there’s an argument to be made that Lucas’s true groundbreaking work — besides unintentionally rewriting the Hollywood business model — lies in the resources he invested in evolving special effects, particularly in the digital age. That’s arguably far more experimental than the non-narrative stuff that he apparently didn’t dabble in as much.

Seems like ILM and Pixar are the true formal fruits of his labor.

>lies in the resources he invested in evolving special effects, particularly in the digital age. 

Certainly, but that falls more under the realm of Lucas-as-producer or as-movie-mogul than Lucas-as-director. Not that there's anything wrong with being a great producer, of course!
